title: Two Sum
description:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. You can return the answer in any order.
simpleExplanation: We are looking for a pair of numbers in the array whose sum equals a given target. We need to return their zero-based index positions.
inputDescription: An array of integers `nums` (length N >= 2) and an integer `target`.
outputDescription: An array containing two integer indices `[i, j]` where `nums[i] + nums[j] === target`.
keyObservation: Instead of searching for nums[j] that equals target - nums[i] by scanning the rest of the array, store previously seen numbers in a Hash Map to look up complements in O(1) time.
hints: Hint 1: If you pick a number `x`, what number `y` do you need so that `x + y = target`?
Hint 2: Can you store the numbers you have seen so far in a data structure that allows fast lookups?
Hint 3: Use a Hash Map mapping `num -> index`. For each number, check if `target - num` already exists in the map.

steps.description: Initialize empty Map {}. Inspect nums[0] = 2. Complement needed: 9 - 2 = 7. Not in map. Store 2 -> 0.
Inspect nums[1] = 7. Complement needed: 9 - 7 = 2. 2 is found in map at index 0! Return [0, 1].

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.idea: Try every pair of numbers using nested loops and check if their sum equals the target.
steps: Outer loop i from 0 to N-1
Inner loop j from i+1 to N-1
approaches.explanation: For each of the N elements, we scan up to N elements. Total operations ~ N^2 / 2.

approaches.name: Optimal (Hash Map)
approaches.idea: Single pass pass using a Hash Map to check for complement presence in constant time O(1).
approaches.explanation: We iterate through the array of N elements exactly once. Each hash table lookup and insert takes O(1) time on average.
approaches.whyItWorks: Trading space for time allows constant time complementary lookups.

solutions.explanation: Maintain a hash map storing value to index mappings. For each number, check if target - current exists in map.
Dictionary key-value pairs store visited values and their index for instant O(1) average lookup.
unordered_map provides O(1) time complexity per lookup.
HashMap stores array values as key and index as value.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Given a string `s`, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
simpleExplanation: Find the maximum length of a contiguous block of characters in string `s` such that no character appears more than once in that block.
inputDescription: A string `s` consisting of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.
outputDescription: An integer representing the length of the longest unique substring.

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc", with the length of 3.
The answer is "b", with the length of 1.

keyObservation: Use a sliding window with left pointer `L` and right pointer `R`. Keep track of character frequencies or last seen indices. When a duplicate character is encountered at `R`, advance `L` past the previous occurrence.
hints: Hint 1: Can you use two pointers to represent a substring window `[left, right]`?
Hint 2: How will you check if a character is already inside the current window?
Hint 3: Use a Set or Map. If `s[right]` is in the set, contract the window by incrementing `left` until `s[right]` is unique.

steps.description: R=3 sees duplicate 'a'. Shrink L to 1. Window becomes [L=1, R=3] ('bca'). Set={'b','c','a'}. MaxLen=3.

approaches.name: Sliding Window Set
approaches.idea: Use a hash set to maintain elements in the current active window s[left..right].
steps: While s[right] is in charSet: remove s[left], left++
approaches.spaceComplexity: O(min(N, M)) where M is alphabet size
approaches.explanation: Each character is visited at most twice (once by right pointer, once by left pointer).

title: Valid Parentheses
description: Given a string `s` containing just the characters `'('`, `')'`, `'{'`, `'}'`, `'['` and `']'`, determine if the input string is valid.
simpleExplanation: Determine if brackets open and close in correct matched sequence and nesting level.
outputDescription: Boolean true if valid, false otherwise.
keyObservation: The last opened bracket must be the first closed bracket. This Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) property dictates using a Stack data structure.
hints: Hint 1: Which bracket must close first when brackets are nested?
Hint 2: Store opening brackets on a Stack.
Hint 3: When encountering a closing bracket, pop from the stack and verify it matches.

approaches.name: Stack Matching
approaches.idea: Push opening brackets onto stack. For closing brackets, pop and verify pair match.
steps: For char in s: if opening push to stack. Else pop and verify match.
approaches.explanation: Single pass through string of length N.

solutions.explanation: Push open brackets, pop and compare for closing brackets.

title: Maximum Subarray
description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the subarray with the largest sum, and return its sum.
simpleExplanation: Find a contiguous segment of the array that yields the maximum possible sum.
keyObservation: Kadane's Algorithm: If current cumulative sum becomes negative, reset current sum to 0 because a negative prefix will only diminish future subarray sums.
hints: Hint 1: Should you keep adding numbers if your current running sum drops below 0?
Hint 2: Reset running sum to 0 whenever it becomes negative.
Hint 3: Maintain max sum seen so far.

approaches.name: Kadane's Algorithm
approaches.idea: Single pass greedy DP algorithm resetting negative prefix running sums.
steps: For n in nums: curSum = max(n, curSum + n); maxSum = max(maxSum, curSum)

solutions.explanation: Kadane's algorithm resetting curSum on negative prefix.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description: You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the `i-th` day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock.
simpleExplanation: Find the maximum price difference prices[sell] - prices[buy] where sell > buy.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price = 1) and sell on day 5 (price = 6), profit = 6-1 = 5.

keyObservation: Track minimum buying price seen so far as you iterate through prices, calculating potential profit at each day.
hints: Hint 1: Keep track of the lowest price seen so far.
Hint 2: For each day, compare current price minus lowest price with max profit.

approaches.name: One Pass Minimum Tracking
approaches.idea: Single pass tracking min price and max profit.
steps: For price in prices: minPrice = min(minPrice, price); maxProfit = max(maxProfit, price - minPrice)

solutions.explanation: Track min buy price and max profit.

title: Linked List Cycle
description: Given `head`, the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it.
simpleExplanation: Check if linked list contains a pointer loop where a node points back to a previous node.
inputDescription: Head node of a singly linked list.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 10^4]

examples.explanation: Cycle exists where tail connects to 1st node.

keyObservation: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm: Use slow pointer (moves 1 step) and fast pointer (moves 2 steps). If there is a cycle, fast will eventually lap slow and they will collide.
hints: Hint 1: Can two runners running at different speeds around a circular track meet?
Hint 2: Advance `slow` by 1 step and `fast` by 2 steps.

approaches.name: Fast / Slow Pointers (Floyd's)
approaches.idea: Two pointers moving at 1x and 2x speed.
steps: While fast and fast.next: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next; if slow === fast return true
approaches.explanation: In cyclic list, fast catches slow within N iterations.

youtube.title: Linked List Cycle - Fast and Slow Pointers

title: Reverse Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list.
simpleExplanation: Flip all pointers so that nodes point to their previous node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 5000]
keyObservation: Maintain prev pointer initialized to null, curr pointer to head. At each step, save curr.next, reverse curr.next to prev, then step forward.
hints: Hint 1: Keep track of `prev`, `curr`, and `next` nodes.

approaches.name: Iterative Pointer Reversal
approaches.idea: Three pointers prev, curr, next to flip links.
steps: While curr: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next

title: Find the Duplicate Number
description:
Given an array of integers `nums` containing `n + 1` integers where each integer is in the range `[1, n]` inclusive.

There is only one repeated number in `nums`, return this repeated number.

You must solve the problem without modifying the array `nums` and using only constant `O(1)` extra space.
simpleExplanation: An array of size N+1 contains values from 1 to N. Find the single duplicate value without modifying array or allocating extra memory.
inputDescription: Array `nums` of length N+1 with values between 1 and N.
keyObservation: Since numbers are 1 to N, treat array indices as nodes of a linked list where `node.next = nums[i]`. The duplicate number is the entry point of the linked list cycle!
hints: Hint 1: Can you model the array as a directed graph where index `i` points to `nums[i]`?
Hint 2: Since there is a duplicate number, multiple indices point to the same value, creating a cycle.
Hint 3: Use Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm to find the start node of the cycle!

approaches.name: Floyd's Cycle Detection
approaches.idea: Find cycle intersection point, then reset slow2 to head and step both at 1x speed to find cycle entrance.
steps: Do: slow = nums[slow], fast = nums[nums[fast]] while slow != fast
While slow != slow2: slow = nums[slow], slow2 = nums[slow2]
approaches.explanation: Two phase cycle detection meets O(N) time and O(1) space constraint without modifying array.
approaches.whyItWorks: Distance from start to cycle entrance equals distance from collision point to cycle entrance.

youtube.title: Find the Duplicate Number - Floyd's Cycle Detection

solutions.explanation: Floyd's cycle detection on index pointer array graph.
